Submission: October, 30, 2026

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This individual engineering datasheet documents my contributions to RadioLink, a project developed by Team 105 for EGR 304 at Arizona State University. It provides an overview of my subsystem's functionality, hardware components, design decisions, and integration with the overall device.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
RadioLink is a portable, off-grid communication device designed to provide dependable wireless messaging during emergencies or in areas without cellular or internet service. The project emphasizes reliability, portability, and ease of use.

Team 105 consists of four engineering students, each responsible for developing an individual hardware subsystem that contributes to the complete device. My subsystem focuses on user controls and temperature monitoring to support RadioLink's functionality.

For additional information regarding the project's objectives, requirements, and overall design, visit the Team 105 RadioLink Report.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
My subsystem incorporates a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller, MCP9700A temperature sensor, and MCP6004 non-inverting operational amplifier for temperature signal processing. Six navigation buttons, a test button, and a red LED provide user interaction and additional functionality or device troubleshooting.

An LM7805 voltage regulator converts the subsystem's 9 V DC input into a regulated 5 V supply. Communication with other subsystems occurs through UART, with a common ground shared between the team's boards.

Readers can explore the following sections for additional technical information:

Block Diagram: Component layout, power distribution, and signal connections.

Component Selection: Component comparisons and selection rationale.

Bill of Materials (BOM): Required components, quantities, and costs.

Electrical Schematic: Detailed electrical connections and circuitry.

Power Budget: Current consumption and power requirements.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram illustrates the individual subsystem responsible for user button inputs and temperature readings for the RadioLink. It demonstrates how the major components of the subsystem are connected, how power is distributed, and how signals travel between the subsystem and the rest of the team's device.

The subsystem receives power from an independent 9V 3A DC power supply, which is regulated to 5V 1.5A through an LM7805 linear voltage regulator. This regulated 5V supply provides power to the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, MCP9700A temperature sensor, MCP6004 operational amplifier, and associated user interface circuitry. Unlike the previous design, each team member's subsystem incorporates its own voltage regulator, with only a common ground shared between the subsystems.

The MCP9700A temperature sensor produces an analog voltage signal that passes through the MCP6004, configured as a non-inverting amplifier, before reaching the PIC's RA0/ADC input for measurement. The non-inverting configuration amplifies the sensor's output voltage while maintaining its polarity, improving the signal's usable range for ADC measurements.

User inputs are provided through six buttons connected to the microcontroller's digital input pins. Additional functionality is supported through a test button and LED indicator. Communication with the rest of the team occurs through Connector 2, which provides UART RX and TX connections for serial communication, along with a common GND connection. Each subsystem maintains independent voltage regulation while sharing a common electrical reference for communication.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Temperature Sensor

  1. Microchip Technologies MCP9700A-E/TO

    • $0.61/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Cost effective Requires ADC conversion Easy through-hole soldering Analog signal susceptible to noise Direct PIC ADC connection

  2. Texas Instruments TMP36GT9Z

    • $1.85/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Wide temperature range Higher cost Simple analog interface Lower specified accuracy at 25°C Compatible with 5V supply

  3. Texas Instruments TMP235A2DBZR

    • $0.56/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Cost effective Difficult for surface-mount soldering Small PCB footprint Different voltage-to-temperature conversion Good specified accuracy (±1.2°C (±2°C))

Choice: Option 1: MCP9700A-E/TO

Rationale: The MCP9700A is not only cost effective, but provides simple and direct integration for the Curiosity Nano that will be used for this part of the product. Although its readings aren't as accurate at the TMP235A2DBZR, readings are still within a ±2°C range, and will have a more reliable method of installation.

Operational Amplifier

  1. Microchip Technologies MCP6004-I/SL

    • $0.53/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Low power consumption supports an efficient subsystem Lower slew rate than the alternatives. SOIC-14 package is manageable for PCB assembly Four amplifiers may be unnecessary if only one temperature signal needs conditioning. Operates directly from the subsystem's 5 V supply

  2. Texas Instruments TLV9004IDR

    • $0.91/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons Lower typical supply current than MCP6004 Four channels may be unnecessary for the current circuit. Includes EMI/RFI filtering features Maximum supply voltage is limited to 5.5 V. Lower maximum input offset voltage improves potential measurement accuracy

  3. Texas Instruments TLV9054IDR

    • $1.14/each
    • Link to product
    Pros Cons 5 MHz bandwidth provides room for future applications Higher power consumption than very low-power alternatives Low input offset voltage supports accurate sensing Higher bandwidth is unnecessary for slow temperature measurements Available in SOIC-14 for PCB integration

Choice: Option 1: MCP6004-I/SL

Rationale: The MCP6004 was selected as the best operational amplifier for the subsystem for its effective balance between low power consumption, cost-effectiveness, and compatibility with the subsystem's design. Its operating voltage range of 1.8–6 V allows it to function reliably with the team's regulated 5 V power supply. Additionally, its rail-to-rail input and output capabilities make it suitable for amplifying the MCP9700A temperature sensor's analog voltage through a non-inverting amplifier configuration before sending the signal to the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano's ADC. In comparison, the TLV9054IDR and TLV9004IDR lack the advantages that the MCP6004 holds.

Voltage Regulator

  1. Texas Instruments LM7805CT/NOPB

  • $1.86/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Provides a stable regulated 5V output Higher cost than competing regulators Easy through-hole soldering with TO-220 package Excess voltage is dissipated as heat Built-in thermal and overcurrent protection May require additional cooling at higher loads
  1. STMicroelectronics L7805CV

  • $1.08/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Lower cost than LM7805 Higher typical quiescent current Regulated 5V output with rated 1.5A capacity Excess voltage is dissipated as heat Easy through-hole soldering May require a heatsink at higher loads
  1. Onsemi MC7805CTG

  • $0.99/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Most cost-effective option Rated output current is limited to 1A Built-in thermal and short-circuit protection Requires adequate thermal management TO-220 package is convenient for PCB assembly No significant efficiency advantage over LM7805

Choice: Option 1: LM7805CT/NOPB

Rationale: The LM7805 was selected for its reliable 5V voltage regulation, compatibility with the subsystem's 9V DC input, and straightforward through-hole installation. Its built-in thermal and overcurrent protection supports dependable operation, while its output current capability is suitable for the subsystem's preliminary power requirements. Although the alternatives offer lower costs, the LM7805 provides a suitable balance of performance, protection, and ease of integration.

9V DC Power Supply

  1. GlobTek WR9HD1000CCP-F(R6B)

  • $10.35/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Provides regulated 9V DC with 1A maximum output Requires access to an AC wall outlet Universal 90–264V AC input Barrel connector must match PCB power jack Standard center-positive barrel connector Limits portability without an independent battery
  1. Pololu 1470

  • $11.41/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Provides stable 9V DC with 1A maximum output Higher cost than GlobTek Universal 100–240V AC input Requires an external AC outlet Standard center-positive barrel connector Additional marketplace shipping costs may apply
  1. Jameco ReliaPro DDU090100J0490

  • $12.89/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Provides 9V DC with 1A maximum output Highest cost of the three options Center-positive barrel connector simplifies integration Limited to 120V AC input Suitable for powering the LM7805 regulator Additional marketplace shipping costs may apply

Choice: Option 1: GlobTek WR9HD1000CCP-F(R6B)

Rationale: The GlobTek power adapter was selected for its cost-effectiveness, regulated 9V DC output, and compatibility with the LM7805 voltage regulator. Its 1A maximum output current is sufficient for the subsystem's preliminary power requirements, while its universal AC input and standard barrel connector simplify integration. Compared to the alternatives, the GlobTek provides a practical balance of cost, reliability, and electrical compatibility for RadioLink.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic illustrates the electrical design of an individual subsystem responsible for measuring surrounding temperature, receiving user inputs, and communicating with the other RadioLink subsystems. The MCP9700A-E/TO temperature sensor measures ambient temperature, while an MCP6004 operational amplifier, configured as a non-inverting amplifier, conditions and amplifies the analog signal before it is processed by the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller.

The subsystem includes four directional buttons (UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT) and two action buttons (ENTER, BACK) for user interaction, along with a test button and red LED for debugging and verification. Power is supplied through a 9 V DC adapter and regulated to 5 V using an LM7805 linear voltage regulator, with a 125 mA fuse providing preliminary input protection. Capacitors are incorporated for power stabilization, signal filtering, and button debouncing. UART communication is established through RA3 and RA4 to transmit and receive information between the team's subsystems, which share a common ground while maintaining independent voltage regulation.

Figure 1: Subsystem schematic for function buttons and temperature sensor.
